title: Incentive-Aligned Multi-Source LLM Summaries
claim: Standard pipelines let adversarial sources corrupt the summary; scoring sources by peer agreement filters them and yields a truthful one.
layout: 2 side-by-side panels, left-to-right, red standard vs green ours, shared query banner
description: A titled figure, 'Protecting AI Overviews Against Strategic Attacks', with a legend (reliable check, faulty warning, adversarial prohibited) at top right. A blue banner below shows the user query 'What should I do in Paris today?'. The left panel is red-tinted, 'Standard LLM Processing'. It has three columns: Sources A–E (A–C green with checks, D yellow, E red), a Compromised overview marked 'Attack successful' and 'Not Truthful', and claims in the summary (two correct, one faulty). A gray box notes there are no truthful incentives. A central 'Our method' arrow leads to the green-tinted right panel, 'Our Method'. Its columns are Scoring (leave-one-out task formation, peer-prediction-style scoring, high effort maximizes score), Source weights (A–C High, D–E Low, with low-weight sources filtered), and a Filtered Summary marked 'Protected overview' and 'Truthful'. Red and green contrast guides the eye.
caption: The TTS framework in action. Unlike a standard pipeline vulnerable to manipulation (left), our method (right) scores sources based on informative peer agreement to filter out weakly supported or adversarial/strategic content and produce a robust summary.
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used in modern search and answer systems to synthesize multiple, sometimes conflicting, texts into a single response, yet current pipelines offer weak incentives for sources to be accurate and are vulnerable to adversarial content. We introduce Truthful Text Summarization (TTS), an incentive-aligned framework that improves factual robustness without ground-truth labels. TTS (i) decomposes a draft synthesis into atomic claims, (ii) elicits each source's stance on every claim, (iii) scores sources with an adapted multi-task peer-prediction mechanism that rewards informative agreement, and (iv) filters unreliable sources before re-summarizing. We establish formal guarantees that align a source's incentives with informative honesty, making truthful reporting the utility-maximizing strategy. Experiments show that TTS improves factual accuracy and robustness while preserving fluency, aligning exposure with informative corroboration and disincentivizing manipulation.
